Long ago, before rivers learned their paths, the world was a bowl of dust beneath a silent sky. In a small village lived Nara, a potter who shaped jars but could not fill them, for no rain had fallen in seven years.

Each night she climbed the tallest hill and placed an empty cup on a flat stone. “Sky,” she whispered, “if you have forgotten us, drink from my cup and remember.”

The stars laughed at first, cold and bright. But one star, the smallest, felt pity. It slipped from the heavens and fell into Nara’s cup as a bead of silver fire.

“Carry me to the mountain’s heart,” said the star, “and I will wake what sleeps there.”

Nara walked three days through thorn and ash. At the mountain, she poured the star into a crack in the stone. The ground trembled. From deep below came a sigh, then a roar, and water burst forth, clear as moonlight.

It ran down the slopes, carving the first river. The village was saved, and Nara’s empty cup became sacred.

That is why, when drought comes, people set cups beneath the stars, hoping one may grow kind enough to fall.

Before rivers learned to run, the world was a bowl of dust beneath a silent sky. In those days, the Moon was a silver fish trapped in a black pond, and every night she beat her tail, longing for water.

A girl named Sela heard the Moon crying. She climbed the tallest cedar with a clay cup tied to her belt. “Why do you weep?” Sela asked.

“I remember the sea that existed before time,” said the Moon. “But the Sun drank it in his pride, and now the earth thirsts.”

Sela waited until dawn. When the Sun rose, blazing and boastful, she held up a mirror of polished shell. The Sun admired himself so fiercely that he leaned close, closer, until one golden tear fell into Sela’s cup.

She carried it down and poured it into the dust. The tear became a spring, the spring became a stream, and the stream began to sing. The Moon leapt from the sky, silver scales flashing, and swam through the newborn river, guiding it toward every valley.

Since then, rivers shine at night because the Moon still swims in them. And each morning, the Sun rises red, ashamed of his thirst, but warming the waters gently.

She dropped a thread of silver light into Nara’s jar. Nara followed it across plains of dust, through a forest of thorns, to a stone mountain shaped like a sleeping giant. There she set down the jar and struck it with her potter’s knife.

The jar broke, and the moonlight spilled into the mountain’s heart. The giant woke and wept, not from sorrow, but from joy at hearing a human song. His tears rushed out as springs, joining hands until they became the first river.

Since then, potters leave one jar unfired beneath the full moon, so if the rivers ever forget their way, the Moon can fill it with silver and guide them home.

Myth: Before rivers carried names to the sea, the world was a clay bowl left too long in the fire. The fields split open, and even the trees held their leaves like closed fists. In a village of dust lived Nara, a potter, who made jars so beautiful that people kept them though nothing remained to store.

Every night she climbed a black hill and set an unfired jar beneath the Moon. “Silver mother,” she prayed, “if water has died, teach me its grave.”

The Moon lowered a ladder of pale light. “Water is not dead,” she whispered. “It is dreaming under the ribs of the mountain. But stone wakes only for what is broken.”

Nara carried her finest jar across the ash plains to the oldest peak. At its summit she sang the first lullaby her mother had taught her, then dashed the jar against the rock. The clay shattered; the moonlight it had gathered spilled like milk into every crack.

The mountain shuddered, opened one blue eye, and began to cry. Its tears became springs, then streams, then a river that curled around Nara’s village like a shining bracelet.

That is why, during drought, people break a small cup at moonrise, reminding the sleeping waters to dream outward.

Since then, people place empty vessels beneath the full moon, for water favors those who believe emptiness can become a beginning..

One night she carried an empty cup to the highest hill. The Moon saw the wave on its rim and lowered a silver thread. “Take this to the mountain with the closed eye,” she said. “But know this: what carries hope must be willing to break.”

Nara walked until dawn burned her shadow away. At the mountain she found a dark seam like an eyelid. She placed the cup against it and sang of rain she had never felt. Then she broke the cup.

Moon-silver flowed into the stone. The mountain opened its eye and wept a river, bright as mercy.

Since then, people break one small cup in drought, so hope may spill forward.

Then she broke the bowl.

Moonlight entered stone. The mountain sighed, opened its blue eye, and the first river ran laughing.

Since then, drought ends when bowls break beneath the Moon.
